e.t: This Hebrew noun identifies people from Egypt, rendered “Egyptians.” It normally describes an Egyptian person or people in Old Testament passages. The word appears 76 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with especially frequent use in Genesis and Exodus. Its contexts include people speaking, acting, being ruled, and interacting with Israelites, so it functions as a national or geographical designation rather than naming a particular individual. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Alammelech refers to a named place in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs once, in Joshua 19:26, and is rendered “Alammelech.” Because this word is preserved as a place-name rather than supplied with an explicit definition, its main function is identification: it distinguishes a particular location in the land. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its exact role in that passage; the word itself primarily names the place.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to adultery or adulterous conduct. It appears twice in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 13:27 and Ezekiel 23:43. In the available scriptural relationships, it is connected with language for committing adultery, which confirms that it names the wrongdoing itself rather than a person or place. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning is the violation of marital faithfulness.

“Nehum” is a personal name in the Hebrew text, not a general descriptive word. It identifies one individual listed in Nehemiah 7:7. This name appears once in the Hebrew corpus, and its normal function is to name a person rather than to express an action, quality, or idea. Since no explicit definition or surrounding verse text is available, the clearest meaning is the individual’s name itself. Its precise significance beyond identifying that person cannot be established from the available lexical information.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a female servant—a woman described in relation to service or household status. It is used throughout the Old Testament, appearing 56 times, and commonly functions as a designation for such a woman rather than as a personal name. Its settings include household life, laws concerning servants, and situations where a woman speaks of herself before God or another person. The surrounding verse determines the precise circumstance, but the central meaning remains a female servant.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to fine linen, a fabric used as a valuable textile. It appears four times in the Old Testament, describing linen connected with clothing or cloth goods. In Judges, it is something offered as part of a prize; Proverbs associates it with merchandise, and Isaiah includes it among fine items. Thus, the word points to a material valued for its quality and usefulness, rather than to an action or abstract idea.

e.t: The word means “Red.” In the Hebrew Old Testament, it functions as a geographical name or description, especially in references connected with a notable body of water and Israel’s departure from Egypt. Its 28 occurrences span several Old Testament books, showing that it is a recurring geographical term rather than a general statement about color in every passage. The exact force in a particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

e.t: Sisamai is a personal name, identifying a person in the Old Testament genealogy. It is not presented as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 2:40, within a family record that connects the person with begetting and genealogy. Its meaning as a name is therefore best understood by the individual it identifies rather than by a separate ordinary-word definition.

This Hebrew noun means “numbers,” referring to counted quantities. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 71:15. In its recorded use, it serves as the object of wording associated with knowing and counting, so it points to quantities that can be reckoned or declared. The precise force in Psalm 71:15 depends on the verse’s surrounding text, but the word’s basic sense remains numerical quantities rather than a person, place, or action.

Azariah is a personal name, identifying a person rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Daniel 2:17, and English Bible renderings preserve it as “Azariah.” Because a personal name identifies someone, its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, rather than on the name alone. Here, the word functions simply as the name of the person being mentioned.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Achan,” referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general action or quality. It functions as a name throughout its six occurrences in the Old Testament Hebrew text, all found in Joshua. The name appears in Joshua 7 and again in Joshua 22, so its precise significance in any one sentence depends on the surrounding passage. As a proper name, it identifies the person being spoken about, addressed, or connected with an event.

This Hebrew word means “ribs,” referring to the bones along the sides of the chest. It functions as a noun naming that part of the body. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 7:5. Because the word appears only there and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its basic meaning can be stated clearly, while its precise significance in that passage depends on the context of Daniel’s vision.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Asaph.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing especially in Chronicles, Nehemiah, Psalms, and related historical records. Its references connect it with people involved in worship, speech, and giving, but the name itself does not describe those activities. The surrounding passage is needed to determine which person named Asaph is intended in a particular verse.

This Hebrew noun means “pot,” naming a cooking container or utensil. It refers to a physical household object rather than an action, person, or quality. The word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with each occurrence describing a pot used in an everyday setting. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete: a pot. The surrounding verse determines the particular use, but the word itself identifies the object.

This Hebrew word means “break,” expressing an action rather than naming a person or thing. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 4:27. Its basic sense is focused and direct: “break.” The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what is being broken in that occurrence, since the verse text is not included here. Thus, readers should understand this word as describing the action of breaking, without extending it to additional meanings.

“Halted” describes someone or something that is not moving normally, especially when movement has been impaired. In its four Hebrew Bible occurrences, this word presents the condition of being halted rather than an action of stopping something else. It can describe a person or a group in a weakened or disabled state. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “holy,” describing what is set apart for God and treated as sacred. It can refer to holy things, places, or appointed occasions rather than only to a personal quality. Its use is especially prominent in Israel’s worship and sanctuary language, where what belongs to God is distinguished from ordinary use. The word occurs 467 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad and repeated pattern of holiness connected with worship, sacred service, and God’s presence.

This Hebrew word describes something as “sure.” It functions as a descriptive term, presenting something as established or certain rather than doubtful. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel: once in Daniel 4:26 and again in Daniel 6:26. Those references identify its limited usage, while the repeated rendering “sure” provides the clearest ordinary meaning for reading the word.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “taches,” naming the connecting items used in the tabernacle’s curtain construction. It appears ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all in Exodus, especially in instructions for joining and arranging the tabernacle curtains. The word therefore identifies a physical component of the sanctuary’s structure rather than an action, quality, or person. Its use is concentrated in the account of building the tabernacle and its furnishings. References include Exodus 26:6, 26:11, 26:33, 35:11, 36:13, and 36:18.

This Hebrew word means “afraid,” describing a person’s condition of fear. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its normal meaning is represented by that single occurrence rather than by a broad range of uses. The word serves as a description of being afraid, not as the name of a person, place, or object. Its precise force in Isaiah 44:8 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “breadth.” It refers to the measure or extent across something—the space from one side to another. In its two Old Testament occurrences, both in Job, it describes physical spaciousness or dimensional extent rather than an action or emotion. The related wording appears in Job 36:16 and Job 38:18, but the exact force in either verse belongs to its surrounding sentence. Its basic idea is the wide span or expanse of something.

e.t: This word is a place-name, rendered “Ramoth,” referring to Ramoth-gilead in the Old Testament. It identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in 1 Kings, 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. In several passages, Ramoth is the object of speech about going to it, receiving it, or fighting for it, so its normal function is to name the place under discussion.

This Hebrew word means “chain,” referring to a linked restraint or binding object. It is a noun used once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel 7:23. Its basic sense is something made of connected links, commonly used to restrain, bind, or secure. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a physical chain rather than an action or quality.

gl: a track or passage-way (as if flowing along)
d: a track or passage-way (as if flowing along)

e.t: This Hebrew word means “path,” naming a path in a sentence. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times in two verses: twice in Psalm 77:19 and once in Jeremiah 18:15. It functions as a noun, identifying the path under discussion rather than describing an action. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a path.

This Hebrew word describes something increasing, becoming greater, or multiplying. It is used three times in the Old Testament corpus, with English renderings of “grow” and “multiplied.” The central idea is increase in size, number, or extent rather than remaining small or unchanged. Because the available passages do not include their surrounding verse text here, the precise aspect of increase depends on each passage’s context.

The word means “twined,” describing material or fabric made by strands being joined together. In its Hebrew Old Testament use, it refers to the construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings, including curtains, screens, hangings, and priestly clothing. It occurs 21 times, all in Exodus, so its normal sense is tied to prepared materials used in the sanctuary. Its precise force in any one verse comes from the object it describes.

Shemida is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Shemida” in the Old Testament. It identifies the same named person in three genealogical passages: Numbers 26:32, Joshua 17:2, and 1 Chronicles 7:19. These occurrences connect the name with family and tribal records, rather than presenting it as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. The available passages preserve the name’s identification, but do not provide a separate lexical definition or explain its underlying name meaning.

The word means “tooth,” referring to the hard part used for biting and chewing. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in Daniel 7, with occurrences in verses 5, 7, and 19. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here. The term itself remains a concrete bodily word rather than an abstract quality or action.

This Hebrew word means “utmost.” It functions as a substantive expression, identifying the furthest degree or limit under discussion rather than describing an action. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Genesis 49:26. Because this word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains a boundary or degree understood as utmost.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “astonied,” describing someone left in a state of stunned astonishment. It functions as a descriptive word for a person’s condition rather than naming an object, action, or place. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it appears only once, in Daniel 3:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense presents a person as overwhelmed and unable to respond normally because of what has been witnessed.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “wave.” It refers to something designated as a wave in Israel’s worship instructions, especially in passages concerning what was presented before the LORD. The word occurs 30 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its repeated use in commands and acts of giving shows that it commonly identifies a specified worship-related object or presentation, rather than describing an emotion or general movement. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.
